definition: Chinese computational linguistics is a subset of computational linguistics; it is the scientific study and information processing of the Chinese language by means of computers.
details: The purpose is to obtain a better understanding of how the language works and to bring more convenience to language applications. The term Chinese computational linguistics is often employed interchangeably with Chinese information processing, though the former may sound more theoretical while the latter more technical. Rather than introducing computational linguistics in a general sense, this article will focus on the unique issues involved with implementing the Chinese language compared to other languages. The contents include Chinese character information processing, word segmentation, proper noun recognition, natural language understanding and generation, corpus linguistics, and machine translation.

explainer.lead: Chinese computational linguistics uses computers to study and process Chinese, from handling individual characters to translating text. It matters because Chinese presents language-specific problems that general computational methods cannot simply overlook. Better solutions can improve language applications while also deepening our understanding of how Chinese works.

tiers.eli5: Imagine teaching a computer to read Chinese like teaching it to sort a big box of building blocks. It has to handle the characters, work out which characters belong together as words, and spot names before it can answer, write, or translate. Chinese computational linguistics is the work behind those steps.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer may build a pipeline that processes Chinese characters, segments words, and recognizes proper nouns before passing text to understanding, generation, or translation components. Corpora provide language data for linguistic study and development. A key pitfall is assuming that methods designed for other languages transfer unchanged, without addressing Chinese-specific character processing and segmentation.
tiers.paperLevel: Chinese computational linguistics is computational linguistics restricted to Chinese: the scientific study and computer-based information processing of the language. Its scope includes Chinese character information processing, word segmentation, proper-noun recognition, natural-language understanding and generation, corpus linguistics, and machine translation. It focuses on issues specific to Chinese rather than general computational linguistics, and no single algorithm or formula defines the field.

explainer.example: Given the text “我爱北京”, a system can process its characters, segment it as “我 / 爱 / 北京”, and recognize “北京” as a proper noun. That structured text can then serve a language-understanding or translation application.

usedIn.name: Machine translation
usedIn.detail: Processes Chinese text for translation between languages.

usedIn.name: Natural-language understanding and generation
usedIn.detail: Enables applications to interpret and produce Chinese.

usedIn.name: Corpus linguistics
usedIn.detail: Uses collections of Chinese text to study the language.

usedIn.name: Chinese character information processing
usedIn.detail: Handles character-level text as a foundation for later language tasks.

explainer.intuition: A computer needs representations and processing steps suited to Chinese before it can analyze or generate the language. The field combines linguistic study with practical techniques for those steps.
howItWorks: Represent and process Chinese character text.
Divide the text into words through segmentation.
Identify proper nouns where recognition is needed.
Use corpora to study Chinese and support processing.
Apply the results to understanding, generation, or machine translation.
explainer.whyItMatters: It addresses problems particular to Chinese instead of treating every language identically. This supports more convenient language applications and a better scientific understanding of Chinese.
misconceptions: It is not simply computational linguistics with Chinese data; its focus is the issues involved in implementing Chinese.
It is broader than word segmentation or machine translation alone.
It is often used interchangeably with Chinese information processing, although the former can sound more theoretical and the latter more technical.
